title: Spherical Simplex Metrics, Angular Links, and Cones

items.title: Spherical Gram simplices and angular links of Euclidean faces
items.statement:
**Spherical Gram simplices.** Let $n\ge0$ and let $C=(c_{ij})_{0\le i,j\le n}$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix with $c_{ii}=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]], [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]). Let $C=LL^{T}$ be its unique Cholesky factorisation with lower triangular $L$ and positive diagonal, and let $u_i\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be the $i$-th row of $L$, regarded as a column vector. Define the **positive cone on the vertices** and the **spherical simplex**
$$K(C):=\Bigl\{\sum_i\lambda_iu_i:\lambda_i\ge0\Bigr\},\qquad \Sigma(C):=K(C)\cap S^n,$$
where $S^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:|x|=1\}$ is the unit sphere ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]], [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]); the **vertices** of $\Sigma(C)$ are $u_0,\dots,u_n$. The definition asserts neither that the $u_i$ are unit vectors with the prescribed inner products, nor that $\Sigma(C)$ lies in a hemisphere, nor any metric statement about it: all of that is proved in [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]].

**Angular link of a Euclidean face.** Let $C$ be a compact convex polyhedral cell in its Euclidean affine hull with direction space $V$, given by finitely many affine inequalities $\ell_j\ge0$, and let $F$ be a nonempty face ([[def-finite-convex-cell-complex-and-linear-subdivision]]). Write $I(F)$ for the set of $j$ with $\ell_j$ vanishing on $F$, $n_j:=\nabla\ell_j/|\nabla\ell_j|$ for the **inward unit normal** of the facet $j$, and
$$U(F):=\operatorname{span}\{x-y:x,y\in F\}\subseteq V$$
for the **direction space of $F$**, the linear span of the differences of points of $F$, which is $\{0\}$ exactly when $F$ is a vertex. The **tangent cone** of $C$ at $F$ is
$$T_FC:=\{\xi\in V:\langle\xi,n_j\rangle\ge0\text{ for all }j\in I(F)\},$$
equivalently the closure of $\{\lambda(x-p):x\in C,\ \lambda\ge0\}$ for any (hence every) $p$ in the relative interior of $F$, and the **normal cone** of $F$ in $C$ is
$$N_FC:=T_FC\cap U(F)^{\perp},\qquad U(F)^{\perp}=\{\xi\in V:\langle\xi,u\rangle=0\text{ for all }u\in U(F)\};$$
the **angular link** of $F$ in $C$ is the set of unit inward directions *normal to $F$*,
$$\operatorname{Lk}_C(F):=N_FC\cap S(V),\qquad S(V)=\{\xi\in V:|\xi|=1\},$$
and the **angular distance** of $\xi,\eta\in\operatorname{Lk}_C(F)$ is $d_{\mathrm{ang}}(\xi,\eta):=\arccos\langle\xi,\eta\rangle$, the principal inverse cosine ([[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]); equivalently it is the intrinsic path metric of the round unit sphere restricted to the link, a metric of diameter at most $\pi$ ([[def-metric-space]]; proved in [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]](v), using that $N_FC$ is a convex cone). For a point $p$ in the relative interior of $F$ the set of *all* unit inward directions at $p$ is $\operatorname{Lk}_C(p):=T_FC\cap S(V)$; when $\dim F=k$ it is the spherical join $S^{k-1}*\operatorname{Lk}_C(F)$ of the round unit sphere of $U(F)$ with the link of $F$, and for a vertex $F$ it coincides with $\operatorname{Lk}_C(F)$ (proved in [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]](4)).

For an isometric polyhedral gluing $X$ with cells $C_p$ ([[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]) the links $\operatorname{Lk}_{C_p}(F)$ of the cells containing a face $F$ are identified along the isometries induced by the gluing maps $h_{p,q}$, giving the **angular link** $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ with the componentwise intrinsic path metric of the cells ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]](1)); the links $\operatorname{Lk}_{C_p}(p)$ of the point $p$ glue in the same way to $\operatorname{Lk}_X(p)$. No new combinatorial link is introduced: the cells of $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ are the unit direction sets normal to $F$ in the cells $G>F$, which are exactly the cells of the combinatorial link of $F$ ([[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]]); this item adds the angular metric to that combinatorial structure.
items.strategy: A definition item. The Gram simplex is built from the Cholesky factor of a real positive-definite matrix with diagonal $1$ (the real case of [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]) and the unit sphere of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]; the angular link is the unit section of the normal cone, obtained by intersecting the tangent cone with the perpendicular of the linear direction space of the face cut out by the inward unit normals of the facets containing the face, and the angular distance is the principal inverse cosine of the inner product. Nothing beyond the construction is asserted: the unit-norm and inner-product properties of the $u_i$, the identity $T_FC=\overline{\mathbb R_+(C-p)}$, the independence of $p\in\operatorname{relint}F$ and of the inequality presentation, the metric axioms of $d_{\mathrm{ang}}$ and the Schur-complement description of vertex links are all proved by the recorded justifier [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]]. The cone and join formulas that consume the link are defined in [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]]. The combinatorial link is imported from [[def-simplicial-subcomplex-star-closure-and-link]] rather than redefined.

items.title: Gram realisations, radial normalisation, finite spherical complexes and link Gram formulas
items.statement:
Let $C=(c_{ij})$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix with diagonal $1$, and let $L$, $u_0,\dots,u_n$, $K(C)$, $\Sigma(C)$ be as in [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]].

**(i) Existence and uniqueness of the Gram realisation.** The vectors $u_i$ are unit vectors with $u_i\cdot u_j=c_{ij}$, they are linearly independent and span $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and every other family $u_i'$ of unit vectors in a Euclidean space with $u_i'\cdot u_j'=c_{ij}$ is the image of $(u_0,\dots,u_n)$ under a linear isometry of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ onto the span of the $u_i'$. Hence $\Sigma(C)$ is well-defined up to an isometry of $S^n$ mapping vertices to vertices.

**(ii) Hemisphere, radial coordinates and bi-Lipschitz comparison.** The linear functional $\varphi$ determined by $\varphi(u_i)=1$ for all $i$ satisfies $\varphi\bigl(\sum_i\lambda_iu_i\bigr)=\sum_i\lambda_i$; consequently $\varphi>0$ on $K(C)\setminus\{0\}$ and $\Sigma(C)$ is contained in the open hemisphere $\{x\in S^n:\varphi(x)>0\}$. Radial normalisation $\rho(x):=x/|x|$ restricts to a bijection $\Delta(C)\to\Sigma(C)$, where $\Delta(C):=\{\sum_i\lambda_iu_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}$, with inverse $y\mapsto y/\varphi(y)$; every point of $\Sigma(C)$ therefore has unique barycentric ray coordinates $\lambda_i\ge0$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. Moreover $\rho$ and $\rho^{-1}$ satisfy the explicit Lipschitz estimates $|\rho(x)-\rho(y)|\le\frac{2}{\min_{z\in\Delta(C)}|z|}|x-y|$ and $|\rho^{-1}(y)-\rho^{-1}(y')|\le(1+\lVert\varphi\rVert)|y-y'|$, proved directly from the formulas without differentiability; hence the round metric $d_{\mathrm{ang}}(\xi,\eta)=\arccos\langle\xi,\eta\rangle$ on $\Sigma(C)$ is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to the Euclidean metric of the compact convex cell $\Delta(C)$ carried by $\rho$ (on a subset of the unit sphere the round distance and the chord distance satisfy $\text{chord}\le\text{round}\le\frac{\pi}{2}\,\text{chord}$).

**(iii) Finite spherical complexes.** *Assume the Axiom of Choice* ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a finite abstract simplicial complex ([[def-abstract-simplicial-complex]]) whose simplices $\sigma$ carry positive-definite Gram matrices $C_\sigma$ of diagonal $1$ on their vertices, compatible with faces. Form the **finite spherical complex** $X:=|K|_C$, the quotient of the disjoint union of the spherical simplices $\Sigma(C_\sigma)$ by the vertex-wise identifications of faces determined by $K$, with the **chain metric** $d$ on $X$: the infimum of $\sum_id_{p_i}(x_{i-1},x_i)$ over finite chains of points in common cells, where $d_{p}$ is the angular metric on the cell $p$; equivalently the infimum of lengths of paths in $X$. Then radial normalisation of the cells descends to a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of $X$ onto the Euclidean isometric polyhedral gluing with cells $\Delta(C_\sigma)$ ([[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]); consequently $X$ is a compact length space whose metric topology is the weak topology, it is proper and complete, and every two points of a connected component of $X$ are joined by a minimizing geodesic of length $d(x,y)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[def-complete-metric-space]], [[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]). The argument is the proper-target one of [[thm-cg-proper-polyhedral-spaces-have-minimizing-geodesics]] rerun on the compact spherical complex, using [[lem-cg-metric-target-length-reparametrization-and-lower-semicontinuity]] and [[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]]. In particular every pair at distance $<\pi$ is joined by a minimizing short path.

**(iv) Vertex and face links by Schur complements.** For $1\le i\le n$ put $v_i:=(u_i-c_{i0}u_0)/\sqrt{1-c_{i0}^{2}}\in u_0^\perp\cap S^n$. The link of the vertex $u_0$ in $\Sigma(C)$ is the spherical simplex with vertices $v_1,\dots,v_n$, and its Gram matrix is
$$c^{\mathrm{lk}}_{ij}=\frac{c_{ij}-c_{i0}c_{j0}}{\sqrt{(1-c_{i0}^{2})(1-c_{j0}^{2})}}\qquad(1\le i,j\le n),$$
which is positive definite: the projection formula follows by expanding $v_i\cdot v_j$, and positivity follows from the positive definiteness of the unnormalised Schur complement $(c_{ij}-c_{i0}c_{j0})_{i,j\ge1}$, whose quadratic form is $w^{T}Cw>0$ for the nonzero vector $w=(-x_1c_{10}-\cdots-x_nc_{n0},\,x_1,\dots,x_n)$. Iterating the formula over the vertices of a face of $\Sigma(C)$ gives the link of that face; the result is independent of the order of iteration, and the link of a face of a link is the link of a higher face.

**(v) Angular links of Euclidean faces.** For a compact convex polyhedral cell $C$ and a face $F$ as in [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]], with direction space $U(F)$ and normal cone $N_FC=T_FC\cap U(F)^{\perp}$, the two descriptions of the tangent cone agree: $T_FC=\overline{\{\lambda(x-p):x\in C,\ \lambda\ge0\}}$ for every $p$ in the relative interior of $F$, and $T_FC=\{\xi:\langle\xi,n_j\rangle\ge0\ (j\in I(F))\}$ for the inward unit normals of the facets containing $F$; the tangent cone and the normal cone depend only on $F$. A convex cone is closed under nonnegative combinations, so for $\xi,\eta\in N_FC\cap S(V)$ the shorter great-circle arc between them stays in $N_FC\cap S(V)$ and realises $\arccos\langle\xi,\eta\rangle$ as an intrinsic path in the link; conversely every path in $N_FC\cap S(V)$ has length at least the round distance of its endpoints. Hence the angular distance of [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]] is the intrinsic path metric of the round sphere restricted to $\operatorname{Lk}_C(F)$, it is a metric of diameter at most $\pi$, and the links $\operatorname{Lk}_{C_p}(F)$ of the cells containing a face $F$ of an isometric polyhedral gluing depend only on $F$, so their quotient $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ is well defined up to canonical isometry.

**(vi) Disconnected components.** If the angular link of a face of a complex is disconnected, the componentwise path distance is $+\infty$ between distinct components; this value is auxiliary notation only and is truncated in the cone formulas of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]].
items.strategy: (i) Existence: read the Cholesky factorisation $C=LL^{T}$ of the real positive-definite matrix and take the rows of $L$; then $u_i\cdot u_j=(LL^{T})_{ij}=c_{ij}$ and $|u_i|^2=c_{ii}=1$, and the $u_i$ are linearly independent because $L$ is invertible. Uniqueness: two families with the same Gram matrix have the same linear relations, so the map $u_i\mapsto u_i'$ extends to a well-defined linear isometry of their spans. (ii) $\varphi(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i$ on $K(C)$ by the basis decomposition; the inverse of $\rho$ is computed from $\rho(x)=x/|x|$ and $\varphi(x)=1$ on $\Delta(C)$. The Lipschitz estimates are the elementary two-line computations $\bigl|\frac{x}{|x|}-\frac{y}{|y|}\bigr|\le\frac{|x-y|}{\min(|x|,|y|)}+\frac{\bigl||y|-|x|\bigr|}{\min(|x|,|y|)}\cdot\frac{|y|}{|y|}\le\frac{2|x-y|}{\min_{z\in\Delta}|z|}$ (with $0\notin\Delta$ because $\varphi\equiv1$ on $\Delta$) and $\bigl|\frac{y}{\varphi(y)}-\frac{y'}{\varphi(y')}\bigr|\le\frac{|y-y'|\,\lVert\varphi\rVert_{\infty}+|y'|\,|\varphi(y)-\varphi(y')|}{\varphi(y)\varphi(y')}\le(1+\lVert\varphi\rVert)|y-y'|$, where $\varphi\ge1$ on $\Sigma(C)$ since $|z|\le1$ for $z\in\Delta$; no differentiability theory is needed. (iii) The Gram matrices of faces are principal submatrices and the Cholesky models are compatible, so the cell-wise radial normalisations agree on faces and descend to a map $\Phi$; the chain metric on $X$ and the chain metric on the Euclidean model bound each other by the two Lipschitz constants (apply $\Phi^{\pm1}$ to a chain), so $\Phi$ is bi-Lipschitz. Compactness comes from the finite union of compact cells with the weak topology ([[prop-a-finite-simplicial-complex-has-compact-hausdorff-realization]] after the compatible triangulation of the cells); properness, completeness and the agreement of the metric and weak topologies transfer from [[thm-cg-polyhedral-chain-metric-topology-and-properness]]. For the geodesic clause take chains from $x$ to $y$ with lengths tending to $d(x,y)$, join consecutive chain points by the unique round geodesic arc inside a common cell (each cell has diameter $<\pi$ because it lies in the open hemisphere), arc-length reparametrise with [[lem-cg-metric-target-length-reparametrization-and-lower-semicontinuity]], apply the proper-target Ascoli theorem [[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]] to the compact target $X$ and lower semicontinuity of length to obtain a limit path with $L(\gamma)=d(x,y)$; the chord bound $L(\gamma)\ge d(x,y)$ is the single-partition sum, so $\gamma$ is minimizing and its arc-length reparametrisation is a geodesic. (iv) Expand $v_i\cdot v_j=\frac{c_{ij}-c_{i0}c_{j0}}{\sqrt{(1-c_{i0}^2)(1-c_{j0}^2)}}$; positivity is the Schur complement computation: for $x\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ the vector $\bigl(-\sum_jc_{0j}x_j,\ x\bigr)$ has $C$-quadratic form $x^{T}C^{\mathrm{lk}}x>0$, so the link matrix is positive definite. Face links are the normalised orthogonal projections onto the complement of the face span. Iteration projects onto perpendiculars of successive residual directions, which are orthogonal, and gives the same positive Schur complement in every order. (v) The normal cone is pointed and closed under nonnegative combinations, so the sector between two of its unit vectors lies in the normal cone and the shorter great-circle arc realises $\arccos\langle\xi,\eta\rangle$ inside the link; the reverse inequality is the chord bound. The two descriptions of the tangent cone agree because a vector $\xi$ satisfies $\langle\xi,n_j\rangle\ge0$ for every facet normal $n_j$ vanishing on $F$ exactly when it is a limit of nonnegative multiples of vectors $x-p$ with $x\in C$, and the facet hyperplanes cut out the affine hull of $F$. (vi) The disconnected convention is recorded for use in the cone formulas, where it is truncated to a finite angular metric.
items.axiom_use: AC is consumed exactly through [[cor-arzela-ascoli-subsequence-theorem-for-proper-metric-targets]] in the geodesic-existence clause of (iii); (i), (ii) and (iv) are choice-free and [[thm-cg-proper-polyhedral-spaces-have-minimizing-geodesics]] records the same AC use for the Euclidean model.

items.title: The angular path metric, the Euclidean cone and spherical joins
items.statement:
**(1) Angular path metric.** Let $L$ be a set with an **extended metric** $d_{\mathrm{path}}:L\times L\to[0,\infty]$, symmetric, vanishing exactly on the diagonal and satisfying the triangle inequality in the extended reals. For the angular link $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ of a face of a finite spherical complex ([[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]], [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]]) the metric $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ is the componentwise intrinsic path distance: the infimum of lengths of finite chains of directions inside a common cell, with $d_{\mathrm{path}}(x,y)=+\infty$ for $x,y$ in different components. The value $+\infty$ is **auxiliary notation only** and is never passed to the published definition of a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

**(2) Truncated angular metric.** With the convention $\min\{\pi,\infty\}:=\pi$, put $d_\pi(x,y):=\min\{\pi,d_{\mathrm{path}}(x,y)\}$. This finite-valued function on $L\times L$ is the **angular metric**; it has values in $[0,\pi]$ and its metric axioms are proved in [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]] ([[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]], [[cor-pi-is-the-first-positive-sine-zero]], [[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]).

**(3) The Euclidean cone.** The **Euclidean cone** on the angular link $L$ is the set
$$C(L):=\{o\}\sqcup((0,\infty)\times L),$$
where $o$ is the **apex**, with
$$d_C(o,o):=0,\qquad d_C(o,(r,x)):=r,\qquad d_C\bigl((r,x),(s,y)\bigr)^2:=r^2+s^2-2rs\cos d_\pi(x,y).$$
In particular $C(\emptyset)=\{o\}$ is a one-point space, not the empty space; and if $d_\pi(x,y)=\pi$ — which happens in particular when $x,y$ lie in different components of $L$ — then $d_C\bigl((r,x),(s,y)\bigr)=r+s$, the length of the path through the apex. The infinite value of $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ is never an ordinary metric value, and the cone receives only $d_\pi$.

**(4) Angular CAT(1) convention.** A link $L$ is **$D_\pi$-geodesic** if every pair of points at distance $<\pi$ is joined by a minimizing segment. Angular CAT(1) statements about a link concern only triangles of perimeter $<2\pi$ and their comparison in the unit sphere $S^2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]); every such test lies in one intrinsic component and agrees with the componentwise intrinsic test of $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ whenever no side equals $\pi$, while a side of length $\pi$ is realised in the model sphere by an antipodal pair; this is proved in [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]].

**(5) Spherical join.** Let $L_1,L_2$ be angular links with metrics $d^1_\pi,d^2_\pi$. The **spherical join** $L_1*L_2$ is the quotient of $L_1\times L_2\times[0,\pi/2]$ by the identifications $(x,y,0)\sim(x,y',0)$ and $(x,y,\pi/2)\sim(x',y,\pi/2)$; write $(\cos\theta)x+(\sin\theta)y$ for the class of $(x,y,\theta)$. The distance of $x=(\cos\theta)x_1+(\sin\theta)x_2$ and $x'=(\cos\theta')x_1'+(\sin\theta')x_2'$ is the unique number in $[0,\pi]$ with
$$\cos d(x,x')=\cos\theta\cos\theta'\cos d^1_\pi(x_1,x_1')+\sin\theta\sin\theta'\cos d^2_\pi(x_2,x_2').$$
Conventions: $L*\emptyset:=L$, $\emptyset*L:=L$ and $\emptyset*\emptyset:=\emptyset$; these are consistent with the product-cone isometry $C(L_1)\times C(L_2)\cong C(L_1*L_2)$, under which $L_1*L_2$ is the unit link of the product cone. Quotient descent to the identified endpoints, the triangle inequality, associativity, the face metrics and the isometry with the unit link are conclusions of [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]]; this item asserts only the construction, the formula and the conventions.
items.strategy: A definition item. It fixes the auxiliary extended metric (with the recorded infinity convention), its finite-valued truncation, the cone formula, the CAT(1) convention and the join formula. The only assertions are the constructions and the conventions $C(\emptyset)=\{o\}$ and $L*\emptyset=L$, $\emptyset*\emptyset=\emptyset$; the metric axioms of $d_\pi$, the metric and geodesic structure of the cone, the agreement of truncated and intrinsic comparison tests, quotient descent, triangle inequality, associativity and unit-link description of the join are all proved by the recorded justifier [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]]. The truncation at $\pi$ is exactly the diameter bound that makes the cone formula a metric, and [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]] supplies the componentwise path metric for links of finite spherical complexes.

items.title: The cone and join metrics, truncation agreement and the local product chart
items.statement:
Let $(L,d_{\mathrm{path}},d_\pi)$ be an angular link with its componentwise path metric and truncated metric as in [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]], and let $L_1,L_2$ be angular links. Then:

**(1) Truncation agreement.** $d_\pi$ is a metric on $L$ of diameter at most $\pi$; it agrees with $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ on every pair at distance $<\pi$; every triple with $d_\pi$-perimeter $<2\pi$ has at most one side equal to $\pi$, and if no side equals $\pi$ then the triple lies in a single component of $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ and its three sides are the intrinsic path distances. Consequently the angular CAT(1) conventions of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]] ($D_\pi$-geodesics and comparisons for perimeter $<2\pi$) coincide with the componentwise intrinsic tests whenever no side equals $\pi$, and a side of length $\pi$ — which can arise only from a pair in different components or at intrinsic distance $\ge\pi$ — is realised in the model sphere by an antipodal pair.

**(2) Cone metric and geodesics.** Clause (3) of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]] defines a metric on $C(L)$, including the cases where one radius is zero, where $d_\pi(x,y)=\pi$ and where $x,y$ lie in different components; the metric is finite-valued and $C(\emptyset)=\{o\}$ is a point. If $d_\pi(x,y)=\pi$ then the path through the apex has length $r+s=d_C\bigl((r,x),(s,y)\bigr)$ and is minimizing. If $d_\pi(x,y)<\pi$ and $x,y$ are joined in $L$ by a minimizing segment, then the development of that segment into the planar sector of angle $d_\pi(x,y)$ is a minimizing geodesic of $C(L)$ from $(r,x)$ to $(s,y)$ of length $d_C\bigl((r,x),(s,y)\bigr)$; if in addition $L$ is $D_\pi$-geodesic, then $C(L)$ is a geodesic space and every minimizing geodesic joining two points of $C(L)$ is contained in the closed ball of radius $\max\{r,s\}$ about $o$ ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]).

**(3) Join, cone and product cone.** Clause (5) of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]] defines a metric on $L_1*L_2$ (descent to the quotient, symmetry and the triangle inequality included) of diameter at most $\pi$; $L_1$ and $L_2$ sit in $L_1*L_2$ as the classes with $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\pi/2$, and the conventions $L*\emptyset=L$, $\emptyset*\emptyset=\emptyset$ are consistent with the construction. The map
$$\bigl((r,x),(s,y)\bigr)\mapsto \xi(R),\qquad R=\sqrt{r^2+s^2},\quad \cos\theta=\frac{r}{R},\quad \sin\theta=\frac{s}{R},$$
where $\xi(R)$ is the point of $C(L_1*L_2)$ at distance $R$ from the apex in the direction $(\cos\theta)x+(\sin\theta)y$, is an isometry $C(L_1)\times C(L_2)\to C(L_1*L_2)$ for the square-sum product metric; consequently $L_1*L_2$ is, up to isometry, the unit link of the product cone, and the join is associative up to canonical isometry. The face metrics of the join are the joins of the corresponding face metrics, and for round unit spheres $S^{m-1}*S^{n-1}\cong S^{m+n-1}$.

**(4) Local product chart.** Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing satisfying the standing hypotheses (H2) local finiteness and (H3) finitely many shapes of [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], and let $p\in X$ lie in the relative interior of a $k$-dimensional cell $F$ ([[def-finite-convex-cell-complex-and-linear-subdivision]]). Then the connected component $X_p$ of $p$ carries its chain metric, and the angular link of the point $p$, that is the set $\operatorname{Lk}_X(p)$ of unit directions of the tangent cone $T_pX$ (the finitely many sets $T_FC_r\cap S(V_r)$ for the cells $C_r$ containing $p$, identified by the gluing), is the spherical join $\operatorname{Lk}_X(p)\cong S^{k-1}*\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$, where $S^{k-1}$ is the round unit sphere of the direction space of $F$; and there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that the metric ball $B_{X_p}(p,\varepsilon)$ in $X_p$ is isometric to the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about the cone point of $C(\operatorname{Lk}_X(p))$ and to the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about $(0,o)$ in $\mathbb R^k\times C(\operatorname{Lk}_X(F))$, these charts preserving intrinsic lengths. In particular the cone receives only the truncated angular metric: the auxiliary value $+\infty$ of $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ is never an ordinary distance value.
items.strategy: Prove truncation and the cone triangle inequality by planar development and the separate angle-sum greater than pi bound. Pull the cone function of the join back from the product cone, then prove the join triangle inequality by testing the metric inequality at radii 1,s,1 with s chosen on the endpoint chord. Establish local radial coordinates using a common inactive-facet radius over the finite incident star, identify the tangent-gluing chain metric with the cosine cone metric by developing chains, and prove the square-sum face product metric by simultaneous constant-speed coordinate paths. Recover the spherical join from unit radial distances.

title: Spherical Simplex Metrics, Angular Links, and Cones — Examples

items.title: A spherical simplex from a Gram matrix and its vertex-link Schur complement
items.statement:
Let $c=\tfrac12$ and let $C$ be the $4\times4$ real symmetric matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and off-diagonal entries $c$. Then:

(i) $C$ is positive definite: for every $x\in\mathbb R^4$, $x^{T}Cx=(1-c)\lVert x\rVert^2+c\bigl(\sum_ix_i\bigr)^2$, which is $>0$ for $x\ne0$ because $1-c=\tfrac12>0$ and $c>0$.

(ii) By [[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]] and [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]](i), the Cholesky realisation gives four unit vectors $u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3\in\mathbb R^4$ with $u_i\cdot u_j=\tfrac12$ for $i\ne j$; the pairwise angular distances in the spherical simplex $\Sigma(C)$ are all $\arccos\tfrac12$, and the barycentric ray coordinates of every point of $\Sigma(C)$ are unique. The functional with $\varphi(u_i)=1$ is the pairing with the vector $w=\tfrac25(u_0+u_1+u_2+u_3)$ (from $C\cdot 1=\tfrac52\cdot1$), and $\varphi\equiv1$ on $\Delta(C)$; hence $\Sigma(C)$ lies in the open hemisphere $\{\varphi>0\}$.

(iii) The vertex link of $u_0$ computed by the Schur formula of [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]](iv) has Gram matrix with entries $\dfrac{c-c^2}{1-c^2}=\dfrac{c}{1+c}=\dfrac13$; explicitly
$$C^{\mathrm{lk}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac13&\frac13\\[2pt]\frac13&1&\frac13\\[2pt]\frac13&\frac13&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad y^{T}C^{\mathrm{lk}}y=\tfrac23\lVert y\rVert^2+\tfrac13\Bigl(\sum_iy_i\Bigr)^2>0\quad(y\ne0),$$
so the link is the spherical triangle with all angular distances $\arccos\tfrac13$, and its positivity is exactly the Schur-complement positivity of [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]](iv).

(iv) Iterating the formula once more gives the link of the face spanned by $u_0,u_1$ as the arc of angular length $\arccos\tfrac14$ between the unit directions of the orthogonal projections of $u_2,u_3$ onto $\operatorname{span}(u_0,u_1)^\perp$: the projected squared norms are $\tfrac23$ and the projected inner product is $\tfrac16$, so the projected cosine is $\tfrac14$, the same value that the two-step Schur computation $\tfrac{1/3-(1/3)^2}{1-(1/3)^2}=\tfrac14$ produces; the formula and the positivity check are otherwise the same, so the face-link computation is order-independent for this matrix.
items.strategy: All four clauses are direct computations. (i) Expand the quadratic form: $x^{T}Cx=\sum_ix_i^2+2c\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=(1-c)\lVert x\rVert^2+c(\sum_ix_i)^2$; the two coefficients are positive, so the form is positive definite and [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]/[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] apply. (ii) The Cholesky realisation provides the unit vectors; the inner product of two of them is $c=\cos(\pi/3)$-free, so the angular distances are described as $\arccos c$ and no special-value theorem is needed; $\varphi$ is obtained by solving $C\varphi$-coordinates, and $\varphi(u_i)=\sum_jC_{ij}\varphi_j$ is checked directly. (iii) Insert $c=\tfrac12$ into $c^{\mathrm{lk}}=(c-c^2)/(1-c^2)$; the quadratic-form identity verifies positive definiteness without any spectral theorem. (iv) The projection formula is applied twice and the two possible orders are compared, using $u_0^\perp\cap u_1^\perp=(u_1^\perp\cap u_0^\perp)$ and the symmetry of the Schur complement in the leading $2\times2$ block; the projected squared norm of $u_2$ is $1-\tfrac13=\tfrac23$, the projected inner product of $u_2,u_3$ is $\tfrac12-\tfrac13=\tfrac16$, and their ratio is $\tfrac14$.

items.title: Link edge lengths versus dihedral mirror angles in type I_2(m)
items.strategy: All clauses are explicit two-dimensional computations. (i) The angle of a regular $2m$-gon is computed by splitting it into the $2m$ isoceles centre triangles. The link of a vertex is the cone spanned by the two incident edge directions, and its unit section is the arc whose angular length is the interior angle; this uses only the definition of the angular link and the angular distance. (ii) Inward unit normals are perpendicular to the edge directions and rotate the angle by $\pi/2$, so the angle between them is $\pi$ minus the interior angle; alternatively the two facet inequalities at the vertex are solved directly. (iii) Insert $c=\cos(\pi/m)$ in the two spanning vectors of the kernels and evaluate $B$ using the Gram matrix; the denominator is $1-c^2>0$ for $0<c<1$ and the numerator is $c(1-c^2)$, so the cosine of the angle is $c$. The rotation statement is the trace computation $A=r_sr_t$ with $\operatorname{tr}A=2\cos(2\pi/m)$ and $A^m=\mathrm{id}$, $A^k\ne\mathrm{id}$ for $0<k<m$ ([[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]]): the only other finite-order isometries of the positive-definite plane are rotations, and the trace identifies the angle $2\pi/m$. (iv) Substitute $\pi-\pi/m$ in $\cos$ and use the addition/shift identities; positive definiteness is the determinant $1-c^2>0$. The last sentence only records the two complementary values.

items.title: The disconnected universal-Coxeter nerve and the angular truncation convention
items.statement:
Let $n\ge2$ and let $L=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ be the **universal-Coxeter nerve**: the finite spherical complex ([[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]](iii)) whose cells are $n$ one-point spherical simplices, the nerve of the Coxeter system on $n$ generators in which $m_{st}=\infty$ for all $s\ne t$, so that no two distinct generators form a spherical pair and the nerve has no edge. Write $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ for its componentwise intrinsic path distance and $d_\pi=\min\{\pi,d_{\mathrm{path}}\}$ for its truncated angular metric ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]]). Then:

(i) every component of $L$ is a single point, $d_{\mathrm{path}}(x,y)=+\infty$ for $x\ne y$, and $d_\pi(x,y)=\pi$ for $x\ne y$. Thus $d_\pi$ is a metric of diameter $\pi$ that agrees with $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ nowhere off the diagonal; the infinite value $d_{\mathrm{path}}(x,y)$ is not an ordinary metric value ([[def-metric-space]]), which is precisely why the truncation is needed.

(ii) In the cone $C(L)$ the distance of $(r,x)$ and $(s,y)$ with $x\ne y$ is $r+s$: the formula of [[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]](3) gives $d_C^2=r^2+s^2-2rs\cos\pi=(r+s)^2$, and the path through the apex realises it. Hence $C(L)$ is the metric star of $n$ rays of infinite length glued at the apex, and every path between two different rays passes through the apex.

(iii) $L$ is vacuously $D_\pi$-geodesic: no pair of distinct points has distance $<\pi$. Hence [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]](2) applies and shows that $C(L)$ is a geodesic metric space, and a geodesic joining points of two different rays is the two-segment path through the apex.

(iv) Any truncation value $\theta<\pi$ would be inconsistent with this star geometry: with distance $\sqrt{r^2+s^2-2rs\cos\theta}<r+s$ between the branches and every path between them passing through the apex, no geodesic would join the two branches, while with the value $\pi$ the through-apex path is one. Thus $d_\pi=\pi$, and not $d_{\mathrm{path}}$, is the value the cone formula must receive, and the auxiliary infinity is never passed to a metric value.
items.strategy: Everything is a direct evaluation of the definitions on a finite discrete metric space. (i) $\min\{\pi,\infty\}=\pi$, and $\min\{\pi,\cdot\}$ of an extended metric is a metric ([[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]](1)); $+\infty$ is not a real number, so it cannot be a value of the published metric-space definition [[def-metric-space]]. (ii) Substitute $d_\pi=\pi$ in the cone formula and use $\cos\pi=-1$; the two-part path through the apex has length $r+s$ by the definition of $d_C$ on the two segments, and it is minimizing by [[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]](2). (iii) The hypothesis of the $D_\pi$-geodesic clause is vacuous because all distinct distances equal $\pi$; with $L$ consisting only of isolated points, the cone is the star and the geodesics are the through-apex segments. (iv) The value $\theta<\pi$ would give the cone distance strictly below $r+s$; but in the star the two branches meet only at the apex, so no path shorter than $r+s$ exists, and the defining formula with a truncated value $<\pi$ would contradict the metric it is supposed to compute. No claim about the Davis complex is made beyond this local model.
